The question of whether stress causes stomach ulcers reflects genuinely conflicting opinions and research outcomes. The American Psychological Association [d5] states flatly that "contrary to popular belief, stress does not increase acid production in the stomach, nor causes stomach ulcers," attributing ulcers to bacterial infection. Similarly, Johns Hopkins Medicine [d7] notes that "in the past, experts thought lifestyle factors such as stress and diet caused ulcers," but that today H. pylori bacteria and NSAIDs are recognized as the main causes. U.S. News [d6] and Granite Peaks GI [d3] reinforce this modern consensus, with [d6] stating "studies to date show that stress alone does not cause peptic ulcers" and [d3] calling the stress-causes-ulcers idea a myth. However, Cleveland Clinic [d1] acknowledges "a lot of conflicting research and debate on the topic," noting stress serves as a backdrop and accomplice, and a PMC/NIH article [d4] presents older theories in which stress-induced noradrenaline secretion and increased stomach acidity were thought to directly contribute to ulcer development. A further distinction is drawn by Medical News Today [d2], which identifies a separate category called "stress ulcers" caused by severe physiological stress, noting that "rarely, very significant psychological stress can trigger a stress ulcer." In summary, the prevailing evidence from high-credibility sources [d5][d6][d7] holds that stress alone does not cause typical stomach (peptic) ulcers, though stress may worsen symptoms or indirectly increase risk, and older or alternative frameworks [d4][d1] have suggested a more direct causal link.
